mathviz has almost no JavaScript API for layout. You put a handful of classes on wrapper `<div>`s -- in Quarto, a fenced div `::: {.ojs-panel}` -- and the library lays the controls out and finds what to enhance. This page is every class and attribute you write yourself, with a live example of each. (The classes the library generates, which you never write, are listed under [Internals](reference/internals.qmd#generated-classes).)

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
VM = window.VM
vmTheme = Generators.observe(notify => VM.plotting.onThemeChange(notify))
chartColors = VM.plotting.colors(vmTheme)
```

## At a glance

| Class / attribute | Put it on | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| [`ojs-panel`](#ojs-panel) | a div around `Inputs.*` cells | the control-panel chrome; restyles every input inside |
| [`ojs-row`](#ojs-row) / [`ojs-grid`](#ojs-grid) | the same div, or a nested one | one wrapping flex row / an auto-fit grid |
| [`ojs-fill`](#ojs-fill) / `ojs-auto` / `ojs-end` | an input's wrapper (`classList.add`) | fill the row / natural width / push to the right edge |
| [`ojs-chart-block`](#ojs-chart-block) | a div around the chart cell(s) | anchor for the legend; what fullscreen enlarges |
| [`ojs-chart-controls`](#ojs-chart-controls) | a div **inside** the block, holding sliders | a bar directly above the chart that comes along into fullscreen |
| [`ojs-svg-block`](#ojs-svg-block) | alongside `ojs-chart-block`, for SVG charts | adds the fullscreen button Plotly charts get from the modebar |
| [`plotly-box-large`](#plotly-box-large) | the Plotly graph div | the one shipped chart size |
| [`vm-swatch vm-swatch-alt`](#vm-swatch) (one modifier per palette color, plus `-accent`) | a `<span>` in prose | tints a color word with the matching palette color |
| [`vm-invalid`](#vm-invalid) | an `<input>` | red border and tint for a field that failed validation |
| [`data-vm-play="off"`](#data-vm-play) | a slider or any ancestor | opt that slider out of the play button |
| [`data-example-field="…"`](#data-example-field) | a `viewof` element | a stable handle for `applyExampleParams` |

## Panels

### `ojs-panel` {#ojs-panel}

The look: padding, border, rounded corners, a surface background, and consistent styling of every input, select and button inside it, with labels stacked above controls so a row of them bottom-aligns.

It is **look only**. Pair it with `ojs-row` or `ojs-grid` for layout. Don't nest one panel inside another (the border and background double up); nest a bare `ojs-row` or `ojs-grid` div instead.

### `ojs-row` {#ojs-row}

One wrapping row, bottom-aligned. The **first** control stretches to fill; the **last** takes its natural width; anything between takes its natural width too. That is the shape of most panels: a wide expression field, then a couple of small controls, then a button.

::: {.ojs-panel .ojs-row}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof rowF = Inputs.text({label: "f(x)", value: "x^2 - 2"})
```
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof rowX0 = Inputs.text({label: "x₀", value: "1"})
```
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof rowGo = Inputs.button("Plot")
```
:::

````markdown
::: {.ojs-panel .ojs-row}
```{ojs}
viewof f = Inputs.text({label: "f(x)", value: "x^2 - 2"})
```
```{ojs}
viewof x0 = Inputs.text({label: "x₀", value: "1"})
```
```{ojs}
viewof go = Inputs.button("Plot")
```
:::
````

### `ojs-grid` {#ojs-grid}

An auto-fit grid of equal columns (about 250 px each; fewer on narrow screens), bottom-aligned. For a panel of several similar controls where none should dominate.

::: {.ojs-panel .ojs-grid}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof gridA = Inputs.range([0, 1], {label: "alpha", step: 0.01, value: 0.5})
```
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof gridB = Inputs.range([1, 50], {label: "n", step: 1, value: 10})
```
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof gridC = Inputs.select(["Euler", "RK4"], {label: "method"})
```
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof gridD = Inputs.checkbox(["show error", "show exact"], {label: "overlay", value: ["show exact"]})
```
:::

### `ojs-fill`, `ojs-auto`, `ojs-end` {#ojs-fill}

Per-control overrides, added to the `viewof` element from the cell that creates it:

```js
viewof expr = {
  const view = Inputs.text({label: "f(x)", value: "sin(x)"})
  view.classList.add("ojs-fill")
  return view
}
```

| Class | Effect |
|---|---|
| `ojs-fill` | Full width; a text input inside becomes a wide box the reader can drag wider -- for a long expression. |
| `ojs-auto` | Natural width, in a row that would otherwise stretch it. |
| `ojs-end` | Pushes the control to the right edge, in a row or a grid. |

## Charts

### `ojs-chart-block` {#ojs-chart-block}

The wrapper around a chart and its companions. A floating [`legendOverlay`](reference/ui.qmd#legendOverlay) is positioned against it, and it is what the **fullscreen button** enlarges -- so a controls bar and legend inside it come along, and the chart keeps its aspect ratio.

Every chart wants one, even a chart that has neither a legend nor controls today. It also lets a chart in a `layout-ncol` column shrink with the column instead of forcing it wide.

### `ojs-chart-controls` {#ojs-chart-controls}

A **direct child** of the chart block, holding the sliders that drive the chart -- an iteration count, a step size. It renders as a bar directly above the chart, stays with the chart in fullscreen, and lays its controls out for that width: fluid slider tracks, compact number fields, labels beside controls.

Sliders in it get the play button. Combine with `ojs-grid` (`class="ojs-chart-controls ojs-grid"`) for several sliders side by side.

::: {.ojs-chart-block}
::: {.ojs-chart-controls}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof ctrlN = Inputs.range([1, 12], {label: "iterations n", step: 1, value: 4})
```
:::
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const g = x => Math.cos(x)
  let x = 1
  const xs = [x], ys = [0]
  for (let i = 0; i < ctrlN; i++) { const gx = g(x); xs.push(x, gx); ys.push(gx, gx); x = gx }
  const curveX = [], curveY = []
  for (let i = 0; i <= 100; i++) { const t = i / 100 * 1.6; curveX.push(t); curveY.push(g(t)) }
  const div = document.createElement("div")
  div.style.height = "300px"
  Plotly.newPlot(div, [
    {x: curveX, y: curveY, name: "cos x", line: {color: chartColors.fn}},
    {x: [0, 1.6], y: [0, 1.6], name: "y = x", line: {color: chartColors.muted, dash: "dot"}},
    {x: xs, y: ys, name: "cobweb", line: {color: chartColors.alt, width: 1.5}, mode: "lines+markers", marker: {size: 5}}
  ], {showlegend: false, xaxis: {range: [0, 1.6]}, yaxis: {range: [0, 1.1]}, margin: {t: 8}})
  VM.plotting.autoResize(div)
  return div
}
```
:::

````markdown
::: {.ojs-chart-block}
::: {.ojs-chart-controls}
```{ojs}
viewof n = Inputs.range([1, 12], {label: "iterations n", step: 1, value: 4})
```
:::
```{ojs}
mainPlot = { ... }
```
:::
````

### `ojs-svg-block` {#ojs-svg-block}

For a chart drawn as inline SVG -- Observable Plot, or a hand-built `<svg>` -- which has no Plotly modebar. Put it **on the same element** as `ojs-chart-block` and nothing else: the library adds a fullscreen button pinned to the top-right corner of the figure, centers the figure in the block, and keeps its aspect ratio in fullscreen. The button survives re-runs of the cell.

The [`VM.discreteMath` page](reference/discrete-math.qmd#live) and the starter's [observable-plot.qmd](https://github.com/apurvanakade/mathviz/blob/main/starter/observable-plot.qmd) use it. Hover the chart there to see the button.

### `plotly-box-large` {#plotly-box-large}

Full width, about three-quarters of the viewport tall with a floor of 500 px (less on a phone). It is the **only** size class shipped -- there is no `-small` or `-medium`. For another height set `div.style.height` yourself, as the examples on this site do.

## Prose

### `vm-swatch` {#vm-swatch}

Tints a word to match a trace: `<span class="vm-swatch vm-swatch-alt">red</span>` gives <span class="vm-swatch vm-swatch-alt">red</span>. The modifier is required; `vm-swatch` alone sets no color.

| Modifier | Token | |
|---|---|---|
| `vm-swatch-fn` | `--vm-color-fn` | <span class="vm-swatch vm-swatch-fn">fn</span> |
| `vm-swatch-alt` | `--vm-color-alt` | <span class="vm-swatch vm-swatch-alt">alt</span> |
| `vm-swatch-ok` | `--vm-color-ok` | <span class="vm-swatch vm-swatch-ok">ok</span> |
| `vm-swatch-muted` | `--vm-color-muted` | <span class="vm-swatch vm-swatch-muted">muted</span> |
| `vm-swatch-ink` | `--vm-color-ink` | <span class="vm-swatch vm-swatch-ink">ink</span> |
| `vm-swatch-warn` | `--vm-color-warn` | <span class="vm-swatch vm-swatch-warn">warn</span> |
| `vm-swatch-accent2` | `--vm-color-accent2` | <span class="vm-swatch vm-swatch-accent2">accent2</span> |
| `vm-swatch-accent3` | `--vm-color-accent3` | <span class="vm-swatch vm-swatch-accent3">accent3</span> |
| `vm-swatch-accent` | `--vm-accent` (the UI accent, not a palette color) | <span class="vm-swatch vm-swatch-accent">accent</span> |

One modifier per palette color, matching the keys of [`VM.plotting.colors()`](reference/plotting.qmd#colors), so a swatch in a sentence and the trace it describes always agree. There is no `-halo`: it is the page background, and a tint of it is invisible.

### `vm-invalid` {#vm-invalid}

A red border and tint on an `<input>` -- for a field whose value failed to parse. **Nothing in the library adds it**; a page toggles it from the cell that validates:

```js
viewof x0 = {
  const view = Inputs.text({label: "x₀", value: "1"})
  view.addEventListener("input", () => {
    const ok = VM.expressions.makeNumber(math, view.value) !== null
    view.querySelector("input").classList.toggle("vm-invalid", !ok)
  })
  return view
}
```

It pairs with [`emptyState`](reference/plotting.qmd#emptyState): the field says *what* is wrong, the chart says *that* something is.

<input class="vm-invalid" value="1/0 + " readonly style="max-width: 12em" aria-label="an input with vm-invalid">

## Data attributes

### `data-vm-play="off"` {#data-vm-play}

On a range slider **or any ancestor**: opt out of the play button. Useful for a slider that isn't a parameter sweep (a zoom level, a seed).

### `data-example-field="<name>"` {#data-example-field}

On a `viewof` element, set by the cell that creates it, as a stable handle for [`applyExampleParams`](reference/ui.qmd#applyExampleParams):

```js
viewof fx = {
  const view = Inputs.text({label: "f(x)", value: "sin(x)"})
  view.dataset.exampleField = "fx"
  return view
}
```

The page's `fieldSelectors` map is then `{fx: '[data-example-field="fx"]', …}`. Selectors rather than references, for a reason that entry explains.
